description: This SIGCOMM 2021 paper investigates the impact of solar superstorms, rare coronal mass ejection events that could cause Internet outages covering the whole globe and lasting several months. It discusses the challenges and available mitigation techniques, then uses real-world datasets to analyse the robustness of the current Internet infrastructure. The main findings are that submarine cables are at greater risk of failure than land cables and that the United States has a higher risk of disconnection than Asia; the paper ends with steps to improve the Internet's resilience. It opens with the estimated economic cost of a day-long US Internet disruption of over $7 billion. Producer: Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi, ACM SIGCOMM 2021, doi 10.1145/3452296.3472916. Coverage: global cable infrastructure. Access: free author PDF; the abstract and introduction were read, and the dataset sources and any code release were not confirmed. Licence and cost: free to read; copyright held by the author. Caveats: the analysis is a scenario study with uncertain storm intensity, not a forecast. Simulation uses: the topology-based failure analysis supports cascading-failure and hazard-exposure models of global connectivity under space weather. Related records: the solar storms and submarine cables case study (case_study-solar-storms-submarine-internet-cables-line-voltage-monitoring) and the NRCan space weather effects chronology (data-nrcan-space-weather-effects-chronology).
